title: Module 2 · Lesson 4 — Prompt and context engineering for agents

lines: Picture an insurance claims agent that takes twenty steps per claim.
Every step re-sends the same long system prompt, plus everything seen so far.
One Monday, an engineer adds the current time to the prompt's first line.
By Friday, every step is slower, and the bill has jumped.
Worse, by step fifteen the agent forgets the policy number, buried under raw documents.
The model is fine; the problem is what it was handed.
A solid system prompt has six parts, from role and scope to termination.
It says what the agent won't do, when to escalate, and what done looks like.
Put everything static at the top, and everything dynamic at the bottom.
A byte-stable prefix lets prefix caching cut time to first token and cost on every step.
That timestamp on line one changed the prefix on every call.
It silently switched the cache off.
The bigger lever is context engineering.
It asks what belongs in the window at this step, and what doesn't.
Big tool results are stored in full, with just a digest and a reference in context.
And the agent sees only the tools for its current phase.
Old turns get replaced by a running summary.
Key facts, like the policy number, live in structured state, so they survive compaction.
Fetch a policy when it's needed, instead of hoping the model recalls it.
Put key evidence at the start and end, because the middle gets lost.
To teach an agent how to choose, examples beat rules.
Show a few full runs, including a tool failure it recovers from, and a moment to ask a question.
A prompt is not a security boundary.
Enforcement belongs in guardrails and tool-level authorisation.
Treat prompts like code: version them, and gate changes on a golden regression set.
A one-word edit can shift tool accuracy by several points.
Exam tip: keep the static prefix byte-identical, because a timestamp at the top quietly breaks prefix caching.
Read on for the full anatomy and every context technique.
